## Where This Fits
**The first week of Part II, and the week that closes W3–W6.** Each of the last four weeks delivered one part: a loss that trains without an alignment (CTC, W3), an encoder whose latency can be computed (the Conformer and streaming, W4), two ways to give the output side a memory (the prediction network and the AED decoder, W4), an encoder that learns without labels (W5), and an alphabet for speech (W6). This week assembles them into a system that has to be *chosen*. The criterion is not "which one has the lowest WER" but one question that runs through the whole week: **where does the language prior live, how strong is it, and how is it combined with the acoustic evidence?** Too little prior and homophones can only be guessed from acoustics (W3's hole); too much and the system hears sentences that were never said (hallucination). The three paradigms sit at three points on this axis: CTC has no prior on the output side (conditional independence; a prior can only be added from outside by shallow fusion), the RNN-T's prediction network is a small prior that has only seen the transcripts of paired data, and the AED decoder is a full language model conditioned on the audio — but trained on the same paired data. Whisper is what an AED looks like after its decoder has read 680,000 hours of transcripts: for the first time the prior is strong enough to speak on its own. LLM-based ASR replaces the prior with an LLM trained on trillions of text tokens and shrinks the acoustic side to an adapter. **Hallucination is not an accident of dirty data; it is a structural consequence of this axis**: $P(\ell \mid \mathbf{X}) \propto P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell)\,P(\ell)$, and when the acoustic evidence is equally flat over all hypotheses (silence, pure noise) the $\arg\max$ is decided by $P(\ell)$ — and a prior trained on transcripts prefers a fluent sentence to the empty string. Read the same axis the other way and it is **biasing**: adding a prior at run time (WFST shallow fusion, deep biasing, prompts). **Decoding** is how the two sides are combined (prefix beam search, fusion weights, subtracting the internal LM). **Evaluation** is the last question: WER counts words and does not say whether the prior or the evidence was right.

The second thread is **supervision**. The Whisper route (large-scale weak supervision) and the wav2vec 2.0 route (SSL plus minutes to hundreds of hours of fine-tuning) are two roads to the same encoder ability; W5 already said "Whisper is not SSL", and this week puts both on one table — data, abilities, failure modes. LLM-based ASR is a third road, with the prior coming from text alone and paired data training only the adapter; RL post-training with WER as the reward (GRPO) is a fourth, and the direct descendant of the sequence-discriminative training of the **YD** era. The third thread is **streaming**: the prior must not look into the future — the RNN-T streams by construction, AED and decoder-only LLMs need segmentation and a read/write policy, and pay for it in WER.

Where the three course-long axes sit this week. **Representation:** all three representations W2 put side by side have now served as ASR input: log-mel (Whisper's encoder reads it directly), continuous SSL features (wav2vec 2.0 fine-tuning, SLAM-ASR's encoder), and W6's discrete units (Chang et al. 2024 feed deduplicated, BPE-compressed k-means units to ASR; DASB finds semantic tokens close to continuous features on ASR and acoustic tokens far behind). And "who decides the frame rate" gets yet another answer: LLM-based ASR stacks the 50 Hz encoder output 4–5 frames at a time before the LLM, so it is the **LLM's token budget** that decides. **Latency:** this week fills the **ASR tail** cell of W1's budget. For a streaming RNN-T the tail is almost only the emission delay (W4 Demo 2 measured a median of 220 ms) plus endpointing; a non-streaming AED or LLM pushes the whole utterance's work to after the user stops, so the tail is the full decode — W1 Demo 2 measured whisper.cpp `small` (Metal) on this machine at a p50 of 68 ms for a six-second Mandarin sentence; for LLM-based ASR the tail is prefill plus first token plus token-by-token generation. **Supervision:** four answers side by side — 680,000 weakly labelled hours, SSL plus ten minutes, a text LLM plus an adapter, RL rewarded by WER.

Four concrete points on the local-language thread. (1) **Mandarin has no word boundaries, so use CER, not WER**; Mandarin–English code-switching (the SEAME family of corpora) uses MER — the same model ranks differently under the three metrics. (2) **Traditional vs. simplified characters is a normalisation issue**: Whisper's Mandarin output switches between the two scripts, so an evaluation that does not convert first reports false errors; a prompt written in traditional characters pushes the output towards traditional — the cheapest use of prompt-based biasing, done in Demo 2. (3) **Language coverage**: Whisper's language table (99 language tokens, 97 languages with training data, Cantonese added in large-v3) has neither Taiwanese Hokkien nor Hakka; MMS has adapters for `nan` (Min Nan) and `hak` (Hakka) among its 1,000+ languages; the Qwen3-ASR technical report lists 22 Chinese dialects including "Minnan" and no Hakka — and whether Taiwan's Taiwanese is in the training data, the report does not say. Local ASR data and evaluation live in the Formosa Speech Recognition Challenge line (TAT, Hakka Across Taiwan). (4) W3 marked "Mandarin homophones make conditional independence bite harder" as my judgement; this week the same Mandarin sentence goes through MMS's CTC (character-level, no LM) and through Whisper, and the homophone substitutions are counted — Demo 3, to be measured.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write CTC, RNN-T, AED and LLM-based ASR as four special cases of one factorisation of $P(\ell \mid \mathbf{X})$, identify for each which term is the output-side prior and what data it was learned from (transcripts of paired data, text alone, or both), and compare the four on latency, controllability (biasing), data requirements and training cost.
2. Write the $p_b$ / $p_{nb}$ recursion of CTC prefix beam search and explain why hypotheses must be merged in prefix space rather than path space (the $\arg\max$ path is not the $\arg\max$ label sequence); write the shallow-fusion decoding objective, derive from Bayes' rule why the internal LM must be subtracted (density ratio), say how ILME and HAT each estimate $P_{\text{ILM}}$, and explain why a length reward exists.
3. Compare weak supervision (Whisper: data construction, the multitask token format, 30-second windows conditioned on previous text) with SSL plus fine-tuning (wav2vec 2.0: ten minutes of labels) in data, ability and failure modes; derive the structural cause of hallucination from "when the evidence is flat, the $\arg\max$ is decided by the prior", and name three triggers (non-speech segments, context carried over in long-form decoding, the decoder's stopping decision) and three countermeasures (VAD segmentation, no-speech thresholds and fallbacks, alignment-driven timestamps).
4. Describe the three families of contextual biasing (contextual WFST / hotwords in shallow fusion, attention-based deep biasing, prompt-based), state at which layer each adds its prior and what each requires (just a list? retraining? only text?), and analyse their usability in streaming and full-duplex systems.
5. Write the alignment DP behind WER and the decomposition $(S + D + I)/N$, state its four problems (normalisation, equal weighting, incomparability across languages → CER / MER, blindness to meaning), classify the errors in an ASR output (S / D / I, hallucination, repetition loops, language misidentification, false errors from normalisation) and trace each back to the paradigm, the decoding or the data.

## References
**Paradigms and overviews**
- Prabhavalkar, Hori, Sainath, Schlüter & Watanabe, **End-to-End Speech Recognition: A Survey**, IEEE/ACM TASLP 32:325–351 (2024; DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2023.3328283; arXiv:2303.03329) — the three paradigms (§II of the arXiv version), LM integration (§VI-B, including internal LM estimation with density ratio and HAT) and contextual biasing (§III-B) in one place; this week's "if you read one paper"
- Graves & Jaitly, **Towards End-to-End Speech Recognition with Recurrent Neural Networks**, ICML 2014, PMLR 32(2):1764–1772 — the first end-to-end CTC system; §5's prefix beam search admits a dictionary and LM through label-level transition probabilities (Eq. 23)
- Watanabe, Hori, Kim, Hershey & Hayashi, **Hybrid CTC/Attention Architecture for End-to-End Speech Recognition**, IEEE JSTSP 11(8):1240–1253 (2017; DOI 10.1109/JSTSP.2017.2763455) — joint CTC / attention training and one-pass decoding scored with the CTC prefix probability (Eq. 48); ESPnet's default
- **JM3** Ch 16 *Automatic Speech Recognition* (2026-08-19 release) — the textbook baseline for CTC, AED and WER
- **YD** Ch 7–8 (sequence discriminative training, adaptation) — discriminative training in the hybrid era, the ancestor of RL post-training

**Decoding and LM integration**
- Hannun, Maas, Jurafsky & Ng, **First-Pass Large Vocabulary Continuous Speech Recognition using Bi-Directional Recurrent DNNs**, arXiv:1408.2873 (2014, preprint) — Algorithm 1: CTC prefix beam search with the $p_b$ / $p_{nb}$ bookkeeping, a word-level LM applied at spaces, and Eq. 8 $p_{\text{net}}(W \mid X)\,p_{\text{lm}}(W)^{\alpha}\,|W|^{\beta}$ (this week's $\lambda$ and $\eta$ are its $\alpha$ and $\beta$); this week's second derivation follows it
- Gulcehre et al., **On Using Monolingual Corpora in Neural Machine Translation**, arXiv:1503.03535 (2015) — where "shallow fusion" and "deep fusion" are named
- Kannan, Wu, Nguyen, Sainath, Chen & Prabhavalkar, **An Analysis of Incorporating an External Language Model into a Sequence-to-Sequence Model**, ICASSP 2018 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8462682; arXiv:1712.01996) — shallow fusion with a coverage penalty on LAS (Eqs. 2–3, penalising incomplete transcripts); shallow fusion only
- Chorowski & Jaitly, **Towards Better Decoding and Language Model Integration in Sequence to Sequence Models**, Interspeech 2017, pp. 523–527 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-343; arXiv:1612.02695) — two problems: over-confident predictions and **incomplete transcripts**, worse once an external LM is added; the fixes are an EOS constraint and a coverage term (Eqs. 9, 11)
- Stahlberg & Byrne, **On NMT Search Errors and Model Errors: Cat Got Your Tongue?**, EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, pp. 3356–3362 (DOI 10.18653/v1/D19-1331; arXiv:1908.10090) — under exact search the empty translation has the best model score for 51.8% of sentences (Table 1, WMT15 En–De): "larger beams are worse" is a model error, not a search error; borrowed here for the length reward and its duality with hallucination
- McDermott, Sak & Variani, **A Density Ratio Approach to Language Model Fusion in End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition**, ASRU 2019, pp. 434–441 (DOI 10.1109/asru46091.2019.9003790; arXiv:2002.11268) — §3.1 states it is "just an application of Bayes' rule to end-to-end models and separate LMs"; §3.4 Eq. 11 adds the target LM, subtracts the source LM and adds a non-blank reward; this week's third derivation follows it
- Meng et al. (10 authors), **Internal Language Model Estimation for Domain-Adaptive End-to-End Speech Recognition**, SLT 2021, pp. 243–250 (DOI 10.1109/SLT48900.2021.9383515; arXiv:2011.01991) — ILME: drop $\mathbf{f}_t$ from the RNN-T joint network and renormalise without blank (§4.1, Eqs. 24–25); remove the context vector in an AED (§4.2, Eq. 31) — "remove the acoustic term", not literally zero the encoder output; Demo 1's third panel on Whisper is its approximation
- Variani, Rybach, Allauzen & Riley, **Hybrid Autoregressive Transducer (HAT)**, ICASSP 2020, pp. 6139–6143 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP40776.2020.9053600; arXiv:2003.07705) — separates the blank Bernoulli (§3.1, Eq. 4) from the label softmax so that the internal LM score $J(\mathbf{g}_u)$ is separable by construction (§3.2) and subtracted in decoding (§3.3, Eq. 9)
- Prabhavalkar, Sainath, Wu, Nguyen, Chen, Chiu & Kannan, **Minimum Word Error Rate Training for Attention-based Sequence-to-Sequence Models**, ICASSP 2018, pp. 4839–4843 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461809; arXiv:1712.01818) — expected WER as the training objective: the step between YD's discriminative training and GRPO

**Contextual biasing**
- Pundak, Sainath, Prabhavalkar, Kannan & Zhao, **Deep Context: End-to-End Contextual Speech Recognition** (CLAS), SLT 2018, pp. 418–425 (DOI 10.1109/SLT.2018.8639034; arXiv:1808.02480) — deep biasing: an LSTM bias encoder embeds the phrases (§3.1), the decoder attends over them and concatenates the result with the acoustic context (Eqs. 6–7), plus a learnable no-bias vector; grapheme-level experiments
- Zhao, Sainath, Rybach, Rondon, Bhatia, Li & Pang, **Shallow-Fusion End-to-End Contextual Biasing**, Interspeech 2019, pp. 1418–1422 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2019-1209) — phrases compiled into a word-level WFST composed with a speller (§2.1), weights pushed to each subword (§2.2), failure arcs that negate the weights already added (§2.2, Fig. 1), biasing applied before beam pruning (§2.3.1)
- Le et al. (12 authors), **Contextualized Streaming End-to-End Speech Recognition with Trie-Based Deep Biasing and Shallow Fusion**, Interspeech 2021, pp. 1772–1776 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2021-1566; arXiv:2104.02194) — shallow fusion, trie-based deep biasing and neural-LM contextualisation combined on a streaming RNN-T
- Lakomkin, Wu, Fathullah, Kalinli, Seltzer & Fuegen, **End-to-End Speech Recognition Contextualization with Large Language Models**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 12406–12410 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10446898; arXiv:2309.10917) — prompt-based biasing: the video title and description prepended as a text prompt before the audio tokens (§1, §3), frozen LLaMA-7B with LoRA

**Weak supervision, SSL fine-tuning, hallucination**
- Radford, Kim, Xu, Brockman, McLeavey & Sutskever, **Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision** (Whisper), ICML 2023, PMLR 202:28492–28518 (arXiv:2212.04356) — data construction (§2.1), the multitask format (§2.3), effective robustness (§3.3), long-form decoding heuristics (§4.5), the normaliser (Appendix C); its cross-attention was Demo 3 in W4
- Peng et al., **Reproducing Whisper-Style Training Using an Open-Source Toolkit and Publicly Available Data** (OWSM), ASRU 2023, pp. 1–8 (DOI 10.1109/ASRU57964.2023.10389676; arXiv:2309.13876) — a Whisper-style reproduction on public data (180k hours for v3, Table 1)
- Peng et al., **OWSM v3.1: Better and Faster Open Whisper-Style Speech Models based on E-Branchformer**, Interspeech 2024, pp. 352–356 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2024-1194; arXiv:2401.16658)
- Peng, Shakeel, Sudo, Chen, Tian, Lin & Watanabe, **OWSM v4: Improving Open Whisper-Style Speech Models via Data Scaling and Cleaning**, Interspeech 2025, pp. 2225–2229 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2025-1062; arXiv:2506.00338) — web-crawled YODAS segmented by CTC, filtered by CTC confidence and by agreement of text and spoken language identification (§2.1): the remedy for "nobody has read these labels", and another 2026 role for CTC
- Koenecke, Choi, Mei, Schellmann & Sloane, **Careless Whisper: Speech-to-Text Hallucination Harms**, FAccT 2024, pp. 1672–1681 (DOI 10.1145/3630106.3658996; arXiv:2402.08021) — about 1% of transcriptions (1.4% in §3; 312 cases) contain hallucinated sentences, 38% of those with explicit harms, 1.7% for speakers with aphasia vs. 1.2% for controls, and hallucinated files have 41% non-vocal time vs. 15% (§4.2); the quantitative evidence for "flat evidence" in this week's first derivation
- Frieske & Shi, **Hallucinations in Neural Automatic Speech Recognition: Identifying Errors and Hallucinatory Models**, arXiv:2401.01572 (2024, preprint) — a working definition of hallucination ("fluent and coherent outputs … entirely disconnected from the input", §1), a three-threshold classifier (WER, semantic similarity, perplexity; Alg. 1) and a noise-injection perturbation test (§3.5)
- Gandhi, von Platen & Rush, **Distil-Whisper: Robust Knowledge Distillation via Large-Scale Pseudo Labelling**, arXiv:2311.00430 (2023, preprint) — §8.4 measures hallucination by repeated 5-grams and insertion error rate; the distilled student has 1.3× fewer repetitions than large-v2; one answer to "how do you measure hallucination"
- Bain, Huh, Han & Zisserman, **WhisperX: Time-Accurate Speech Transcription of Long-Form Audio**, Interspeech 2023 (arXiv:2303.00747) — VAD cut & merge into ≤ 30 s segments; wav2vec 2.0 CTC alignment for timestamps (also cited in W3)
- Zusag, Wagner & Thallinger, **CrisperWhisper: Accurate Timestamps on Verbatim Speech Transcriptions**, Interspeech 2024, pp. 1265–1269 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2024-731; arXiv:2408.16589) — retokenization so that pauses land on space tokens, DTW over cross-attention for timestamps; 1% noise-only clips with empty transcripts in training and dropping tokens shorter than 50 ms at inference; no harmful hallucinations on Koenecke et al.'s AphasiaBank files (§4.3.4, qualitative)
- Baevski, Zhou, Mohamed & Auli, **wav2vec 2.0**, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv:2006.11477) — Table 1: fine-tuning on 10 min / 1 h / 10 h / 100 h of Libri-light (the abstract says "feasibility"); cited in W5
- Likhomanenko et al. (8 authors), **Rethinking Evaluation in ASR: Are Our Models Robust Enough?**, Interspeech 2021, pp. 311–315 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2021-1758; arXiv:2010.11745) — cross-dataset evaluation: only the average WER over enough benchmarks is a proxy for real-world noisy data

**LLM-based ASR and 2025–2026**
- Fathullah et al., **Prompting Large Language Models with Speech Recognition Abilities**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 13351–13355 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10447605; arXiv:2307.11795) — 80 ms conformer outputs stacked $n$ at a time and projected into LLaMA-7B, with LoRA; an early version of the recipe
- Ma et al. (11 authors), **An Embarrassingly Simple Approach for LLM with Strong ASR Capacity** (SLAM-ASR), arXiv:2402.08846 (2024, preprint) — frozen encoder and LLM, only the projector trained ($s_{\text{a}} = 5$ frame stacking, Linear–ReLU–Linear); encoders from Whisper to HuBERT X-Large and LLMs from TinyLLaMA to Vicuna-7B swept; this week's generic LLM-ASR recipe
- Yu, Tang, Sun, Chen, Tan, Li, Lu, Ma & Zhang, **Connecting Speech Encoder and Large Language Model for ASR**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 12637–12641 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10445874; arXiv:2309.13963) — three connectors compared (stacked fully connected, cross-attention, Q-Former); the Q-Former wins with 80 tokens (§6.2)
- Tang et al., **SALMONN: Towards Generic Hearing Abilities for Large Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.13289) — a window-level Q-Former as the adapter (one query per 17-frame window of about 0.33 s, 88 tokens per 30 s; Whisper and BEATs encoders)
- Chu et al., **Qwen2-Audio Technical Report**, arXiv:2407.10759 (2024) — an encoder initialised from Whisper-large-v3, pooled with stride 2 to about 40 ms per frame (25 Hz, §2), attached to Qwen-7B; **a technical report, cited as a preprint**
- Qwen Team (Xian Shi et al., 30 contributors), **Qwen3-ASR Technical Report**, arXiv:2601.21337 (2026) — 0.6B / 1.7B models, an AuT encoder downsampled 8× to 12.5 Hz, 52 = 30 languages + 22 Chinese dialects (Minnan included, no Hakka), context tokens in the system prompt for biasing (trained in by SFT), streaming through a dynamic 1–8 s attention window, and a non-autoregressive forced aligner that predicts 80 ms timestamp indices directly (not CTC); **a technical report, cited as a preprint**
- Qwen, the `Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B` model card (Hugging Face; **not a paper**) — the list of 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects (Minnan included), streaming on the vLLM backend only, and in the same table a higher average WER for streaming than offline (0.6B 4.40 vs. 3.48; 1.7B 3.33 vs. 2.69)
- Tsunoo, Futami, Kashiwagi, Arora & Watanabe, **Decoder-only Architecture for Streaming End-to-end Speech Recognition**, Interspeech 2024 (arXiv:2406.16107) — speech prompts from a blockwise encoder grow the decoder prefix block by block, with CTC blank-dropping as compression
- Wan et al., **Streaming Speech Recognition with Decoder-Only Large Language Models and Latency Optimization**, ICASSP 2026 (arXiv:2601.22779) — speech segments interleaved with text; a read/write policy network with MoChA decides the segment boundaries
- Tang, Puri, Watanabe & Mukherjee, **TRADE: Transducer-Augmented Decoder for Speech LLM**, arXiv:2606.08486 (2026, preprint) — a frame-synchronous transducer branch added to a speech LLM (the LLM's hidden states serve as the prediction network), so one checkpoint decodes both offline and streaming — W4's RNN-T returns in another form
- Kumar et al. (8 authors), **When Synthetic Speech Is All You Have: Better Call GRPO**, SLT 2026 (arXiv:2607.08409) — GRPO with $1 - \text{WER}$ as the reward for domain adaptation of an LLM-based ASR (WavLM-Large + Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct); mostly reduces insertions, by calibrating when to stop
- Chen, Hu, Yang, Siniscalchi, Chen & Chng, **HyPoradise: An Open Baseline for Generative Speech Recognition with Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv:2309.15701) — an LLM generates the transcript from a 5-best list after the fact: a fifth place for the prior
- Chang et al., **Exploring Speech Recognition, Translation, and Understanding with Discrete Speech Units: A Comparative Study**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 11481–11485 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10447929; arXiv:2309.15800) — W6's units as ASR input: k-means on WavLM-large layer 21, deduplication then BPE (LibriSpeech sequences 60% shorter), WER between FBank and continuous SSL features (Table 1)
- Mousavi et al., **DASB**, TMLR 2026 (cited in W6) — the ASR column: semantic tokens close to continuous features, acoustic tokens far behind

**Evaluation**
- Morris, Maier & Green, **From WER and RIL to MER and WIL: Improved Evaluation Measures for Connected Speech Recognition**, Interspeech 2004 (ICSLP), pp. 2765–2768 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2004-668) — WER's upper bound is $\max(N_1, N_2)/N_1$, not 1 (§1, with a 200% example); MER and WIL
- Gillick & Cox, **Some Statistical Issues in the Comparison of Speech Recognition Algorithms**, ICASSP 1989, pp. 532–535 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.1989.266481) — the McNemar test (independent errors, isolated words) and the matched-pairs test (dependent errors, connected speech)
- Kim, Arora, Le, Yeh, Fuegen, Kalinli & Seltzer, **Semantic Distance: A New Metric for ASR Performance Analysis Towards Spoken Language Understanding**, Interspeech 2021, pp. 1977–1981 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2021-1929; arXiv:2104.02138) — the distance between reference and hypothesis in a sentence-embedding space; W14 returns to it
